decisions.final: A board is allocating capital across two departments, Consumer Credit Cards and Consumer Purchase Loans, whose returns are imperfectly (less than perfectly) correlated. Stand-alone 99% VaR is USD 90 million for Consumer Credit Cards and USD 110 million for Consumer Purchase Loans, so that without any diversification benefit the two departments would require USD 200 million of risk capital between them. Taking the diversification effect into account, the combined risk capital requirement is USD 150 million. Following standard practice, the portfolio effect is allocated pro rata with stand-alone risk capital. What is the fully diversified capital of each department?
decisions.reason: Source M2 (p.29) has the same wording; its source note (p.30) confirms the numbers were rebuilt. Re-derived: zero-correlation aggregate sqrt(90^2+110^2)=142.13; combined 150 implies rho=(150^2-90^2-110^2)/(2*90*110)=+0.116, so 'negatively correlated' contradicts the stem's own numbers and the Q23 rule (aggregate above the zero-correlation floor implies positive correlation). Pro rata arithmetic 67.5/82.5 and key (b) verified; key unchanged. OR-T1-24 carries no numbers, so it can keep its wording.

decisions.final:
A bank's Audit and Risk Committee is reviewing the performance of USD 100 million of new loans written during the year. The RAROC projected at initiation was 8.23%. The actual RAROC measured at year end was negative 1.40%. The Chairman has asked the finance department and internal audit to explain the variance. Both were given the following parameters, all expressed as percentages of the loan amount except the return on economic capital, which is the rate earned on the economic capital itself:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Economic capital | 40% |
| Expected revenue | 7% |
| Return on economic capital | 0.5% |
| Expected credit loss on loans | 3% |
| Operating costs | 2.5% |
| Effective tax rate | 30% |

Sector-wide credit spreads narrowed during the year.

**Finance department:** the RAROC was miscalculated because the initial estimate did not factor in expected losses; in addition, actual operating costs came in at double the anticipated amount.

**Internal audit:** the initial RAROC calculation was accurate; the variance was driven by macroeconomic and systematic factors across the sector rather than by any budgeting error.

Which position is *most likely* to be correct?
decisions.reason: Source (pp.13-14) is verbatim the same, so this is a source ambiguity. Re-solved: with 0.5% applied to EC=40, (7-2.5+0.2)*0.7/40=8.225% and (7-3-5+0.2)*0.7/40=-1.40%, which match the quoted figures; with 0.5% read literally as a share of the loan (as the lead-in says), the results are 8.75% and -0.875%, which match nothing. Since the item works by reproducing the quoted figures, the lead-in has to carve out this row (OR-T1-20 already does). Used the auditor's first proposed wording. Key (a) is unchanged.
